claim: An EASAC working group on genome editing recommends that regulators should focus on specific applications of genome editing techniques rather than attempting to regulate genome editing itself as a new technology.
source: An EASAC working group on genome editing recommends that regulators should focus on specific applications of these new techniques rather than attempting to regulate genome editing itself as a new technology.
evidence: This is stated as a recommendation from the EASAC working group in the abstract.

claim: There has been significant progress in the field of plant breeding over the past three decades, with a number of new molecular techniques being introduced.
source: There has been significant progress in the field of plant breeding over the past three decades, with a number of new molecular techniques being introduced.
evidence: This is a general statement about historical progress in plant breeding.

claim: The increased precision now possible in plant breeding using genome editing technologies represents a big change from conventional breeding approaches that relied on random, uncontrolled chemical- or radiation-induced mutagenesis.
source: The increased precision now possible in plant breeding using genome editing technologies represents a big change from conventional breeding approaches that relied on random, uncontrolled chemical- or radiation-induced mutagenesis.
evidence: This compares genome editing precision to conventional mutagenesis approaches based on established knowledge of these techniques.

claim: Emerging opportunities in plant sciences include the simultaneous edits of multiple genes to increase crop quality by developing cultivars with improved water and nitrogen use efficiency, better resistance to pests and diseases, and reduced allergens.
source: Emerging opportunities in plant sciences include the simultaneous edits of multiple genes to increase crop quality by developing cultivars with improved water and nitrogen use efficiency, better resistance to pests and diseases, and reduced allergens (see, for example, Bortesi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bortesi et al., 2016.

claim: One of the first products to be allowed in the US is the CRISPR-Cas9-edited mushroom which has reduced browning due to the decreased activity of polyphenol oxidase.
source: One of the first products to be allowed in the US is the CRISPR-Cas9-edited mushroom (which has reduced browning due to the decreased activity of polyphenol oxidase)
evidence: This is a factual statement about a specific regulatory approval and the mechanism of the trait.

claim: Regulators should confirm that the products of genome editing, when they do not contain DNA from an unrelated organism, do not fall within the scope of GMO legislation.
source: In our opinion, regulators should confirm that the products of genome editing, when they do not contain DNA from an unrelated organism, do not fall within the scope of GMO legislation.
evidence: This is stated as an opinion/recommendation from the authors.

claim: The aim should be to regulate the agricultural trait/product rather than the technology by which it is produced.
source: We also advise that while there should be full transparency in disclosing the process used, the aim should be to regulate the agricultural trait/product rather than the technology by which it is produced.
evidence: This is stated as advice/recommendation from the authors.

claim: Research on animals is already subject to stringent regulation regarding animal health and welfare.
source: Research on animals is already subject to stringent regulation regarding animal health and welfare.
evidence: This is a statement about existing regulatory frameworks.

claim: Animal research is subject to the principles of the '3Rs' (replacement, reduction and refinement).
source: It is also subject to the principles of the "3Rs" (replacement, reduction and refinement), with refinement perhaps being most relevant in this context.
evidence: This refers to established principles in animal research ethics.

claim: Most genome-edited animals are currently being generated for basic or biomedical research purposes.
source: Although most genome-edited animals are currently being generated for basic or biomedical research purposes, there are also significant opportunities for livestock and aquaculture – to enhance animal health and welfare as well as to increase agricultural production.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of genome-edited animal applications.

claim: There are significant opportunities for genome editing in livestock and aquaculture to enhance animal health and welfare as well as to increase agricultural production.
source: Although most genome-edited animals are currently being generated for basic or biomedical research purposes, there are also significant opportunities for livestock and aquaculture – to enhance animal health and welfare as well as to increase agricultural production.
evidence: This is a statement about potential applications based on inference from current research directions.

claim: Recent research is conferring protection from porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome, economically the most important disease affecting pigs in Europe, North America and Asia.
source: For example, recent research is conferring protection from porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome, economically the most important disease affecting pigs in Europe, North America and Asia (Whitworth et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Whitworth et al., 2016.

claim: Porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome is economically the most important disease affecting pigs in Europe, North America and Asia.
source: For example, recent research is conferring protection from porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome, economically the most important disease affecting pigs in Europe, North America and Asia (Whitworth et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the economic importance of the disease, supported by the citation.

claim: Livestock breeding should be governed by the same principles as proposed for crop plant breeding: to regulate the trait and not the technology, and to be open and explicit about what is being done.
source: We recommend that livestock breeding should be governed by the same principles as proposed for crop plant breeding: to regulate the trait and not the technology, and to be open and explicit about what is being done.
evidence: This is stated as a recommendation from the authors.

claim: There is considerable laboratory research underway to develop cellular and animal, including larger animal, models of human disease.
source: There is considerable laboratory research underway to develop cellular and animal, including larger animal, models of human disease.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of research.

claim: The concurrent multiple edits that are now feasible can help to reconstruct complex disease pathways in model organisms to identify and characterise therapeutic targets for functional screening.
source: The concurrent multiple edits that are now feasible can help to reconstruct complex disease pathways in model organisms to identify and characterise therapeutic targets for functional screening.
evidence: This is an inference about the potential applications of multiple concurrent edits based on the capabilities of the technology.

claim: It will be possible to introduce more predictive safety testing and new precision medicine regimens using genome editing.
source: Additionally, it will be possible to introduce more predictive safety testing and new precision medicine regimens (Fellmann et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim about future possibilities is supported by a citation to Fellmann et al., 2017.

claim: Genome editing is helping to transform prospects in xeno-transplantation, by tackling barriers to the transfer of tissues and organs from animals to treat loss or dysfunction in patients.
source: Genome editing is also helping to transform prospects in xeno-transplantation, by tackling barriers to the transfer of tissues and organs from animals to treat loss or dysfunction in patients (Perota et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Perota et al., 2016.

claim: Genome editing can remove the various xeno-reactive animal tissue epitopes, which would otherwise trigger both hyperacute and delayed rejection, and endogenous retroviruses.
source: In particular, genome editing can remove the various xeno-reactive animal tissue epitopes, which would otherwise trigger both hyperacute and delayed rejection, and endogenous retroviruses.
evidence: This is a statement about the capabilities of genome editing in addressing specific barriers to xenotransplantation.

claim: Genome editing is being explored in research on human-animal chimeras (for example growing a pig embryo with a human pancreas) to provide a source of human organs for transplantation.
source: Also, as discussed in the EASAC report, genome editing is being explored in research on human-animal chimeras (for example growing a pig embryo with a human pancreas) to provide a source of human organs for transplantation.
evidence: This is a statement about current research directions as discussed in the EASAC report.

claim: Editing is important in human-animal chimera research to inactivate specific human developmental genes to prevent any contribution to the chimera beyond the organ to be transplanted.
source: Editing is important here to inactivate specific human developmental genes to prevent any contribution to the chimera beyond the organ to be transplanted.
evidence: This is an inference about the role of editing in controlling chimera development.

claim: Gene drive is a process of biased inheritance that enables a gene to be transmitted from parent to offspring at an increased rate.
source: Gene drive is a process of biased inheritance that enables a gene to be transmitted from parent to offspring at an increased rate.
evidence: This is a definition of gene drive based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Applications of genome editing for insect disease vector control and other modifications of target populations may offer significant potential to help address major public health challenges.
source: Such applications of genome editing, for insect disease vector control and other modifications of target populations, may offer significant potential to help address major public health challenges (Alphey, 2016).
evidence: This claim about potential is supported by a citation to Alphey, 2016.

claim: There are efficacy questions still to be answered by research regarding gene drives, such as to what extent genetic diversity in natural populations provides a source of resistance to the gene drive.
source: There are efficacy questions still to be answered by research. For example, to what extent does genetic diversity in natural populations provide a source of resistance to the gene drive?
evidence: This is a statement about outstanding research questions.

claim: If self-sustaining, the spread of gene drive constructs may have ecological consequences beyond those intended.
source: If self-sustaining, will the spread of gene drive constructs have ecological consequences beyond those intended?
evidence: This is posed as a safety consideration question, implying speculation about potential risks.

claim: Recent recommendations by the US National Academies provide a sound framework for responsible development of gene drive applications.
source: Recent recommendations by the US National Academies (National Academies, 2016) provide a sound framework for responsible development of the application.
evidence: This is an evaluative statement about recommendations from the National Academies, supported by citation.

claim: EASAC endorses the US National Academies' emphasis on the importance of a phased approach to research to allow sufficient time to evaluate the efficacy and safety of gene drives before regulatory decisions are made.
source: EASAC endorses their emphasis on the importance of a phased approach to research to allow sufficient time to evaluate the efficacy and safety of gene drives before regulatory decisions are made on whether or not they will be suitable for use.
evidence: This is stated as an endorsement by EASAC.

claim: A recent meeting of the UN Convention on Biological Diversity rejected calls for a moratorium on gene drives but encouraged caution in field testing and supported better risk assessment.
source: The issues are of global relevance: a recent meeting of the UN Convention on Biological Diversity rejected calls for a moratorium on gene drives but encouraged caution in field testing and supported better risk assessment (Callaway, 2016).
evidence: This is a factual statement about a UN meeting outcome, supported by citation to Callaway, 2016.

claim: Genome editing augments and extends the technologies previously available for the genetic alteration of microbes but does not raise significant new ethical or regulatory issues.
source: Genome editing augments and extends the technologies previously available for the genetic alteration of microbes but, in our view, it does not raise significant new ethical or regulatory issues here.
evidence: This is stated as the authors' view/opinion.

claim: There is a wide range of potential applications of genome editing in microbes including biosynthesis of pharmaceuticals, other high-value chemicals and biofuels, and as biosensors, in bioremediation, and in the food chain.
source: There is a wide range of potential applications in microbes (including biosynthesis of pharmaceuticals, other high-value chemicals and biofuels, and as biosensors), in bioremediation, and in the food chain.
evidence: This is a statement about potential applications based on knowledge of microbial biotechnology.

claim: Concerns have been expressed that microbial research may come to be conducted outside of the regulated laboratory setting, for example by the Do-It-Yourself biology community.
source: Concerns have been expressed (Ledford, 2015) that microbial research may come to be conducted outside of the regulated laboratory setting, for example by the Do-It-Yourself biology community
evidence: This claim about concerns is supported by a citation to Ledford, 2015.

claim: The Do-It-Yourself biology community is active in developing responsible research norms.
source: but it has also been said that this community is active in developing responsible research norms (Kuiken, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kuiken, 2016.

claim: It has been recommended by the previous President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology in the US that misuse of technologies such as CRISPR must now be taken into account when setting biodefence strategy.
source: In other policy developments, it has been recommended, for example by the previous President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology in the US (PCAST, 2016) that misuse of technologies such as CRISPR must now be taken into account when setting biodefence strategy, to prepare for combatting state-sponsored terrorism or other misuse of the technology.
evidence: This claim about recommendations is supported by a citation to PCAST, 2016.

claim: Regulatory options for genome editing are being discussed as part of the ongoing scientific underpinning of the Biological and Toxin Weapons Convention.
source: Regulatory options are also being discussed as part of the ongoing scientific underpinning of the Biological and Toxin Weapons Convention.
evidence: This is a statement about ongoing policy discussions.

claim: EASAC together with other academies will convene a workshop to explore the nature and extent of the biosecurity implications of genome editing.
source: Later this year, EASAC together with other academies will convene a workshop to explore the nature and extent of the biosecurity implications of genome editing.
evidence: This is a statement about a planned future activity.

claim: Genome editing is providing new tools for drug discovery by establishing better screening approaches in vitro and in animal models.
source: In addition to providing new tools for drug discovery, by establishing better screening approaches in vitro and in animal models, and by supporting new biosynthetic pathways to generate complex molecules
evidence: This is a statement about current applications of genome editing in drug discovery.

claim: Genome editing is being employed for novel gene- and cell-based therapies in healthcare (somatic cell editing).
source: genome editing is being employed for novel gene- and cell-based therapies in healthcare (somatic cell editing) and could directly correct heritable disease-causing mutations in germline interventions (Fellmann et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fellmann et al., 2017.

claim: Genome editing could directly correct heritable disease-causing mutations in germline interventions.
source: genome editing is being employed for novel gene- and cell-based therapies in healthcare (somatic cell editing) and could directly correct heritable disease-causing mutations in germline interventions (Fellmann et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim about potential is supported by a citation to Fellmann et al., 2017.

claim: It is vital for basic research on genome editing to proceed intensively, subject to appropriate legal and ethical rules and standardised practices.
source: According to our working group and other similar initiatives (Academy of Medical Sciences, 2016; National Academies, 2017), it is vital for basic research to proceed intensively, subject to appropriate legal and ethical rules and standardised practices.
evidence: This recommendation is supported by citations to Academy of Medical Sciences, 2016 and National Academies, 2017.

claim: According to current rules, if early human embryos or germline cells undergo genome editing in the process of research, the modified cells must not be used to establish a pregnancy.
source: In particular, according to the current rules, if early human embryos or germline cells undergo genome editing in the process of this research, the modified cells must not be used to establish a pregnancy.
evidence: This is a statement about existing regulatory rules.

claim: Proposals to use genome editing on human somatic cells for clinical research and treatment should be rigorously evaluated within the current regulatory frameworks for gene and cell therapies.
source: Proposals to use genome editing on human somatic cells for clinical research and treatment should be rigorously evaluated within the current regulatory frameworks for gene and cell therapies, with each case assessed for its potential benefits and risks, such as those that might arise from inaccurate editing.
evidence: This is stated as a recommendation from the authors.

claim: Risks from inaccurate editing apply when contemplating the application of genome editing to human germline cells.
source: These risks also apply when contemplating the application of genome editing to human germline cells, but there are many additional considerations to take into account when predicting potentially harmful effects.
evidence: This is an inference about risks extending from somatic to germline applications.

claim: Additional considerations for germline editing include the obligation to consider the interests of the individual and future generations who will carry the genetic alteration.
source: These include the obligation to consider the interests of the individual and future generations who will carry the genetic alteration, and the concern that the scope of applications might be widened beyond the prevention and treatment of disease to include biological enhancement.
evidence: This is stated as an ethical consideration for germline editing.

claim: There is concern that the scope of germline editing applications might be widened beyond the prevention and treatment of disease to include biological enhancement.
source: These include the obligation to consider the interests of the individual and future generations who will carry the genetic alteration, and the concern that the scope of applications might be widened beyond the prevention and treatment of disease to include biological enhancement.
evidence: This is stated as a concern about potential future applications.

claim: EASAC shares the view that it would not be acceptable to proceed to germline interventions unless and until the relevant scientific, ethical, safety and efficacy issues have been resolved and there is broad societal consensus.
source: EASAC shares the view that it would not be acceptable to proceed to germline interventions unless and until the relevant scientific, ethical, safety and efficacy issues have been resolved and there is broad societal consensus.
evidence: This is stated as EASAC's position on germline interventions.

claim: The latest recommendations from the US National Academies are ambitious in raising the prospect of identifying circumstances in which clinical research trials would be permissible for germline genome editing.
source: The latest recommendations from the US National Academies are ambitious in raising the prospect of identifying circumstances in which clinical research trials would be permissible for germline genome editing (National Academies, 2017).
evidence: This is a characterization of National Academies recommendations, supported by citation.

claim: The US National Academies' recommendations for permissible germline genome editing trials include circumstances with a compelling clinical purpose and stringent oversight system.
source: These circumstances would include a compelling clinical purpose and stringent oversight system.
evidence: This describes specific criteria from the National Academies recommendations.

claim: The US National Academies' recommendations on germline editing are likely to continue to elicit controversy worldwide.
source: Notwithstanding these rigorous criteria, it is likely that such recommendations will continue to elicit controversy worldwide.
evidence: This is a prediction about the reception of the recommendations.

claim: It is vital to ensure that there is no general restriction on basic research and methodological development that would limit clarification of genome editing technology's potential.
source: While these matters are debated (The Lancet, 2017), it is vital to ensure that there is no general restriction on basic research and methodological development that would limit clarification of the technology's potential.
evidence: This is stated as a recommendation, with reference to ongoing debate cited in The Lancet, 2017.

claim: There are cross-cutting issues relevant to the progression of all applications of genome editing including better engagement between scientists and the public-at-large as well as with policy makers.
source: In addition to the sector-specific elements for assessment and regulation, there are cross-cutting issues relevant to the progression of all of the applications of genome editing (and other emerging technologies in the biosciences). There has to be better engagement between scientists and the public-at-large as well as with policy makers.
evidence: This is stated as a need for improved engagement.

claim: Scientists must continue to articulate the objectives for their research, the potential benefits, and the risk-management practices adopted.
source: Scientists must continue to articulate the objectives for their research, the potential benefits, and the risk-management practices adopted.
evidence: This is stated as an obligation for scientists.

claim: Additional social science and humanities research is warranted to underpin improved public engagement strategies for genome editing.
source: At the same time, additional social science and humanities research is warranted to underpin improved public engagement strategies.
evidence: This is stated as a recommendation for future research.

claim: The scientific community must work with others to ensure that an increasing uptake of genome editing technologies does not accentuate inequity in access to the benefits.
source: The scientific community must also work with others to ensure that an increasing uptake of these technologies does not accentuate inequity in access to the benefits.
evidence: This is stated as a responsibility for the scientific community.

claim: There is a responsibility to clarify to policy makers the broader consequences of their specific decisions about regulation and innovation.
source: Furthermore, there is a responsibility to clarify to policy makers the broader consequences of their specific decisions about regulation and innovation.
evidence: This is stated as a responsibility, likely of the scientific community.

claim: Previous decisions in the EU on genetic engineering technologies with respect to GMOs in agriculture have created difficulties for scientists, farmers and politicians in developing countries.
source: For example, previous decisions in the EU on genetic engineering technologies with respect to GMOs in agriculture have created difficulties for scientists, farmers and politicians in developing countries.
evidence: This is stated as a factual consequence of past EU decisions.

claim: EASAC is of the view that policy considerations should focus on sector-specific applications rather than on genome editing itself as an emerging technology.
source: To reiterate, EASAC is of the view that policy considerations should focus on sector-specific applications rather than on genome editing itself as an emerging technology.
evidence: This is stated as EASAC's position.

claim: It is important to avoid inadvertently constraining innovation in genome editing.
source: It is important to avoid inadvertently constraining innovation.
evidence: This is stated as a principle for policy development.

claim: The assessment and regulation of genome editing applications must be evidence-based, must take into account the likely benefits as well as any hypothetical risks, and must be proportionate and sufficiently flexible to cope with future advances in the science.
source: The assessment and regulation of applications must be evidence-based, it must take into account the likely benefits as well as any hypothetical risks, and it must be proportionate and sufficiently flexible to cope with future advances in the science.
evidence: This is stated as a set of principles for assessment and regulation.
